steps.title: Your stop marks where you're wrong
steps.text:
A good stop-loss isn't a random distance, or the amount you can "afford" to lose. It goes where the reason for the trade **no longer holds**.

For a buy at support, that's **below** the support zone.

steps.title: Give it room
steps.text:
Put the stop **beyond** the zone and its wicks, with a small buffer.

A stop inside the zone, or right on an obvious round number, is likely to be hit by normal wiggles even when your idea was right.

steps.prompt: You want to buy here. Tap the support zone: your stop would go just below it.
steps.explanation: The support zone is where the dips kept stopping. A stop **just below it** is only hit if support really breaks.

steps.question: Where does a stop-loss for a short (sell) trade at resistance usually go?
steps.explanation: A short at resistance is wrong if price breaks **above** resistance, so the stop goes just above the zone.

steps.title: Other logical places
steps.text:
• Beyond the most recent **swing low** (for a buy) or **swing high** (for a sell).

• Beyond a **trendline** your trade depends on.

• A multiple of the market's typical daily range (its volatility). You'll meet this in the Indicators level.

steps.question: The logical stop is far away, so your 1% risk only allows a small position. What should you do?
options: Move the stop closer so you can trade bigger
Accept the smaller position, or skip the trade
steps.explanation: The stop comes from the chart; the size comes from the stop. Never squeeze a stop just to trade bigger.

steps.title: Never move a stop further away
steps.text:
You can move a stop **closer** to lock in profit. Never move it **further away** to avoid a loss.

That turns a small, planned loss into a big, unplanned one.

points: Stops go where the trade idea is **wrong**.
Place them **beyond** zones, swings or trendlines, with a buffer.
Size comes from the stop, **not** the other way round.
